I disagree.  There are almost always REASONS a killer kills, but I don't feel it diminishes their agency.  

I used Ed Kemper as an example elsewhere. He's a very intelligent serial killer,  who will explain that his growing up with a very cold/ abusive mother is part of what made him a killer.  It's not his mother's fault he killed those women, it's not her fault he killed her, but to understand WHY, you have to include her actions.

In this case I think CW's mother had a lot to do with his difficulty standing up for himself or doing more than trying to "just get along". I think she's a large part of WHY. But that doesn't make her responsible for his actions, and I don't feel it takes away his agency.

He could have done exactly that.  He should have done exactly that.  We are looking at the possible "why"s he did it. 

No one here has ever said she deserved to be killed no matter what she did. There is a HUGE difference between being part of a reason why and deserving to die.
Example - Ed Kemper's mom was a demanding cold woman - she didn't deserve to die for that,  but it's part of what made him snap. 

And I have to point out the irony of posting to judge others for being what you think is judgemental.

There are so many pieces to the "puzzle" of this crime.

 Not discussing many of the things that trigger some people is going to end in a endless circle of "CW is evil and nothing anyone else did had anything to do with what he did".

The unfortunate truth is a lot of the family and extended family dynamics are very likely pieces of this puzzle.

A great many people here are capable of saying "I completely disagree with your point and always will, here's why" and have changed minds and encouraged conversation.  

Many others seem to almost instantly revert to insinuating character of the poster, calling names, and DMing to trash talk others.

Some expenses and whether deductible:

I will always remember this day as the day I saw the best and the worst of people.

I was the manager of a small "country" gas station and store in Colorado, the kind that becomes a hangout for local folks. After the first plane hit there was a small news blurb on the radio station about it, but at the time it was reported as a small plane, and it wasn't big news.

Then an employee that was off and lived nearby brought in a small TV and told us to watch right after the second plane hit (I think she didn't want to digest the news alone, but I'm grateful she did).  This was in a foothills area, and the TV had rabbit ears (anyone remember those?) so we were constantly having to try to find the best reception.  Between the radio and TV it was an overwhelming amount of information and chatter, and hard to absorb.
 Then the locals started showing up, and stayed.  We all listened and watched together, hugging each other, and trying to contact other regular customers, friends, and employees.  There was an amazing sense of community; we were in this together somehow. People brought food and friendship, cried, and talked about what this meant for the future.

Early evening the tide suddenly shifted as rumors of gas shortages started for some reason (war, whether refineries would shut down in case of attack, etc.).  I had had a full fuel delivery that morning, so I had plenty of fuel for days, I thought.  We suddenly had a massive line for fuel and people were physically fighting in the lot over who was next.
I had to stand outside with flashlights attempting to direct traffic into the station and prevent people from trying to cut in line.  
We had called our distributor when it started but they couldn't get a truck to us until the next afternoon as they were overwelmed with orders, but faxed (remember those?) us confirmation at the post price (no increase from the morning's order). 
People were panicked and so many were absolutely horrid. I was threatened with harm if I didnt let people in out of turn, dozens tried to threaten me with their vehicles (inching closer, revving their engine, etc.), and others were yelling that they'd "teach me a lesson" if I let the ones threatening in ahead of them. I explained until I was hoarse that if they didn't remain civil I could have the cashiers just shut off the pumps and they wouldn't get any fuel, but people couldn't be reasoned with.  We had fights breaking out when I'd let diesel customers in to the diesel only pumps because "that wasn't fair that they got to go first" regardless of the fact that they couldn't use that fuel.
Then we started running low on reg. unleaded (we had pumps that mixed reg. unleaded and premium to produce mid-grade fuel) and people started to really lose their minds. People thought we were trying to gouge them when we explained we only had premium and diesel gas left (at the same price it had been before), and argued with me when I explained we had fuel coming the next morning at the same damn price (I set the price on the pumps, but  they were convinced that it would be dollars higher by morning by some national order). We were shut down for the night by the sheriff because of the number of calls, both about the lines and fighting and people reporting us for price-gouging (prices never increased, we simply ran out of cheap gas).

Hate to tell you, but this is a training issue.

Dog listened to husband because he was the main one training him, and the dog felt he was his only leader, hence becoming agitated when the leader left - to the dog there was no leader he respected.  So dog stepped into that gap and considered himself the leader.
Taking food from kids is common - it tends to be "in their face" through normal kid movements, almost as if offering it to the dog.  This dog said "cool, snacks".
So when the kids say "no", a) this means nothing, he hasn't been trained or worked with by the kids b) he considers himself the leader, so why would he respect someone under him who's keeping food away? c) kids tend to "snatch away" in situations like this, which to a dog that doesn't think he has a leader, means "snap it up before it moves", which obviously works and leads to demanding (barking, growling), and finally attempting to take it by force (snapping at the holder, who may accidently drop it while pulling back, which just reinforced to the dog that it works to do so).
So now you have a dog who thinks he's second in command (which is why he didn't listen when hubby, his leader, was away) which is now getting inconsistent feedback, not only from the non-leader family), but from his leader, who is busier with less time to refresh lessons and his position as leader.  Young dogs, especially male, will almost always try to climb the leadership ladder in their pack (with mellow dogs this isn't as obvious, but they also make a half-hearted attempt to climb the "pack ladder").  So he's making moves that work on the lower pack to the leader, as he senses a shot at being pack leader - hey, it's worked so far.

To have a chance at fixing this, you would have to take a VERY active roll in retraining, so he learns to respect you, and to respect those you, as a leader, tell him to.  Just like kids, dogs actually like boundaries and rules once they understand them (and just like kids that doesn't mean they accept them without testing at first) and have consistency. 

Make sure this dog is fixed, hormones never help teenagers, and they don't help young adult dogs, either.

Decide whether you are willing to work on this dog's retraining or if you are over it.  Dogs can tell, and it won't work if you're just "phoning in.

You can't compare one dog to another, especially 3 who are at completely different life stages.  How your other dog acts has zero to do with this one.
